opus-5.5.text:
I think code plays a very fundamental role, maybe more fundamental than people first realize.

On one level, code is just one important application. Programming is a domain where the model can create a lot of value directly: writing software, debugging, maintaining large codebases. Because the output is verifiable (you can run it, test it, see whether it works), it's also a very good environment for reinforcement learning. You get relatively clean reward signals, which is rare in the real world.

But on a deeper level, I see code as a kind of universal interface between the model and the world. When an agent writes code, it's not only producing text; it's taking actions. It can call tools, manipulate files, process data, browse, and build other tools for itself. In a sense, code is the language through which the model's intelligence gets turned into real operations. A lot of tasks that don't look like programming, like data analysis, research, or even making a slide deck, can actually be decomposed into writing and executing code.

So for agents, coding ability is a foundation for general agentic ability. If a model can reason well over long horizons in a coding environment, planning, trying something, reading the feedback, correcting itself, then a lot of that capability transfers to other kinds of tasks. The coding environment trains the loop of thinking, acting, and observing, which is the core of being an agent.

There's another interesting angle: code lets the model extend itself. Humans became much more powerful because we built tools. If a model can write its own tools, its capability is no longer bounded by what's in its weights. That's why I think scaling agents, letting the model act over longer horizons and use more tools in a more autonomous way, is closely tied to getting code right.

Of course there are still challenges. Real-world software engineering involves very long context, ambiguous requirements, and collaboration with people, and current models are still far from a strong human engineer in many of those dimensions. But the direction is very clear to me: code is one of the most important bridges from a model that can talk to a model that can actually get things done.

fable-5.1.text:
I think code is probably the most important substrate for agents right now, and for a few reasons that go beyond "coding assistants are a good market."

The first is that code is the most verifiable domain we have. If an agent writes a function, you can run the tests. You can compile it. You get a signal that is cheap, fast, and mostly objective. That matters enormously for reinforcement learning, because the whole bottleneck in scaling RL is finding environments where the reward isn't noisy or gameable. Math and code are the two places where that's most true today, and code is the one that connects directly to real economic work.

The second is that code is a universal interface to the world. Almost any task an agent needs to do, whether it's analyzing data, calling an API, controlling a browser, or orchestrating other tools, can be expressed as writing and executing a program. So instead of building a special tool for every action, you give the model a shell and an interpreter and it composes what it needs. When we built Kimi K2 we leaned into this. Agentic capability was not a separate feature, it was mostly about getting the model to use code and tools fluently in long multi-step trajectories.

The third point, which I think people underrate, is that code is how an agent extends itself. A model that can write code can build its own tools, write its own scaffolding, and in some sense improve its own workflow. That is the beginning of a loop where the capabilities compound. Long-term, I think the interesting question isn't "can the agent write code," it's "can the agent use code to keep making itself more capable over long horizons."

So I'd put it this way. Language is how agents understand intent. Code is how they act on it. And the gap between those two is where most of the progress in the next couple of years is going to come from.

astra-6.text:
I think code is important because it gives an agent a general way to act. If you only give a model a fixed set of tools, what it can do is constrained by those tools. But if it can write and execute code, it can combine tools, transform data, and build new capabilities for the task at hand.

Code also gives you a feedback loop. The model writes something, runs it, observes an error or a result, and revises its approach. That lets it test some of its assumptions against an environment rather than just produce an answer that sounds plausible.

So I wouldn’t think of coding as just one application of agents. It can be part of the foundation for more general agents. The challenge is making that process reliable: knowing what to execute, checking whether the result actually meets the user’s goal, and operating within appropriate permissions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think code is a very natural way for an agent to take action. Language is useful for understanding a goal and deciding what to do, but code lets the agent express a precise procedure, execute it, and check the result.

For example, if you ask an agent to analyze some data, it can write a program, run it, inspect the output, and revise its approach. That creates a feedback loop between reasoning and the environment. The agent can test whether its idea actually works.

So I see code as more than a capability for software engineering. It’s a general interface for using tools and automating tasks. The challenge is making that execution reliable: choosing the right actions, catching errors, and knowing whether the result satisfies the user’s goal.
